utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies, and Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to greet everyone in the courtroom. May the Lord bring peace to this court, and I hope that today's proceedings will conclude in compliance with divine providence and not according to my wishes. And I would like to wish the witness a nice and pleasant stay in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday we looked at the map and you drew a triangle to which you were denied access. Today let's continue the problems that you faced with regard to the access that you were denied. First of all, can you tell us first why were you forbidden to move within the Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that -- that was arranged with the DutchBat II. They had a problem there. The reports were that the VRS came forward in that area. Bravo, the observation post I showed you yesterday was not manned, and ABiH wanted DutchBat to man that OP. CO of DutchBat II decided he was not able to do that due to the weather. There was a hell of a lot of snow, and that was the trigger, in fact, that they said, Okay. If you don't man it, then we'll man it ourselves and you're not allowed to come in that area. That's, in short, the reason why there was no freedom of movement in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber, please, the date when this blockade was imposed, and if you cannot remember the exact date, can you just tell us the month.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. This would have been about a week after I arrived, so it would have been the end of January. More or less around the 20th or 25th of January, 1995. And I take it that you refer to the blockade of the patrols we spoke about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you. Let me remind you of an event, but I would like you to tell us what you know about it. Was that event related to the activities that we discussed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For that purpose can we please have document 1D32 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you give the number again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It's 1D32, 1D32. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Registrar gave a number, but it was not heard.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please look at it and as soon as you see the English version, I'm going to read page 1. It actually has only one page. It was drafted on the 17th of February, which is after the date that you mentioned, that is after January, and it reads as follows, and I'm reading the first paragraph: "According to intelligence information, the aggressor is grouping forces and equipment around the demilitarised zones of Srebrenica and Zepa, particularly in the sector of Milici and Vlasenica." This is what you mentioned in your answer as reported to you. This document was signed by Brigade General Enver Hadzihasanovic. Second paragraph reads: "We estimate that the aggressor will start offensive combat operations with the aim of completely overpowering the Milici-Podravanje road and then attempt to seize the territory of the demilitarised zones." The second sentence in the second paragraph: "On the 16th of February, 1995, the aggressor filed a request with UNPROFOR to declare Zepa a non-demilitarised zone with the following rationale: "... helicopter flights have been registered, and I repeat, helicopter flights have been registered. "BH Army have been bringing in ammunition and weapons; secondly, movement of the BH Army have been registered in the Zepa sector. Then: "Accusing members of the Ukrainian Battalion, they're covering up for the activities and intentions of the BH Army, which is why they're no longer guaranteed safety." And the next bullet point: "On the night between 15th --" I repeat. "On the night between 15th and 16th February, 1995, our helicopters were seen flying over and that infantry fire was opened on them." I'm going to skip the next paragraph, and I'll move to the next one: "On the basis of the aforementioned, the aggressor informed the Sarajevo sector and UNPROFOR command that unless Zepa was declared a demilitarised zone, they would start offensive combat operations within seven days. The ultimatum is for 23rd of February, 1995. "According to report of the Ukrainian Battalion from Zepa, the UNPROFOR BH command took the following actions: "Helicopter reconnaissance of the protected Zepa zone was scheduled for 17 February 1995, but the aggressor did not allow it. "A visit by the Ukrainian Colonel Kozub, deputy commander of," I repeat, "a visit by the Ukrainian Colonel Kozub, deputy commander of the UNPROFOR Sarajevo sector, was announced for 18 February 1995." And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please scroll down so that we can see what it reads. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, he's issuing an order as follows: "Units of the Operations Group 8," which was your zone, "are to be in full combat readiness enabling them to be fully prepared to resist a possible attack by the aggressor. "Units of OG 8 deployed in Srebrenica to be on standby for co-ordinated action with the 1st Zepa Light Brigade." We'll skip number 3 and go to number 4 which reads: "Until the helicopter is evacuated, take full measures for camouflaging it, and security measures as ordered." Number 5: "Should the helicopter be found, in your contacts with UNPROFOR representatives, take the position that its purpose was to transport political representatives of Srebrenica and Zepa who were to take part in the work of the political organs." Full stop. Thank you. Now, I purposefully read out this order in order to see that there is a connection between Srebrenica-Zepa, because some of the measures pertain to one and some pertain to the other. Were you informed by the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo that the VRS had requested or wanted an ultimatum to seize and suspend all flights, otherwise combat operations would be launched? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I was not informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you seen in this order that the forces deployed in Srebrenica were tasked with launching a co-ordinated action in the event of an attack?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I just read that. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can one infer from this order that the VRS did not lie when they said that supplies had been brought in by helicopters, because this helicopter crashed in the area of Zepa, and that there was also an instruction here to the effect of how to camouflage the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can infer anything, but I did not know anything about that, so I can't really answer your request.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me were there any helicopter flights from Tuzla to Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but there was a report of, if I remember it correctly, OP Mike, by night there should have been passing a helicopter. We had been looking for that helicopter or that place where it should have been landed. We couldn't find it. We searched the old area directly eastly of Slatina. It's a village at the western border of the enclave. But I don't know exactly the date anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, can you tell us if there were any attacks, as you said, by the VRS on the enclave which prompted you to set up your OPs? And I'm talking about the month in which blockade was imposed on you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we are talking about, say, January, and just for the record, to set up my OPs, my OPs were all 24 hours, seven days a week operational. So there's no question of setup. You could refer to an incident that took place in that period as well, again a report that the VRS came forward opposed to the Bandera Triangle, and we then sent in to the northern border of that Bandera Triangle because there is the location we were told that the VRS came into the enclave. We made a blocking position with two APCs. Arriving there, nothing was seen. There was no contact. We left them there about two, three days and then withdrew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now see document 1D30, 1D30, in e-court. Thank you. We can see the document in both languages. I'm going to read it now. "Due to the situation in the sector of Podgaj, created on the 9th of 1995, of which you were informed in a timely manner, the command of the 8th Operations Group has restricted the movement of the UNPROFOR forces in the wider region of Suceska and Podgaj. "At 1100 hours today, the commander of the Dutch Battalion in Srebrenica ordered his patrols to enter the movement restriction area in co-ordination with the commander of the 8th Operations Group. Respecting the agreement reached with the UNPROFOR liaison officer after the warning was issued not to move in the aforementioned area, the commander of the 281st Eastern Bosnia Light Brigade blocked all UNPROFOR controls and is still keeping them blocked. It was requested by the Dutch Battalion commander that this area immediately be visited by the UNPROFOR commander for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and representatives of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Main Staff and the 2nd Corps command in order to find a peaceful solution to the situation which has developed in the Podgaj village sector and the wider area of Suceska, i.e., the area of responsibility of the 281st Brigade. "We kindly ask that you immediately instruct us on further steps to take regarding UNPROFOR. "Commander, Naser Oric."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This letter was drafted on the 28th of January, 1995, and my question is as follows: Does this refer to the situation that you described yesterday when you were ordered to leave the triangle?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, that refers to the patrols I described yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us now how important that was for ABiH army in Srebrenica, because it appealed to the highest authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that they requested military structures to come and solve this problem. Why didn't they take up this problem with you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know how important it was for the ABiH, because I think you should ask them. And they did take up the problem, because yesterday I told you when I proposed my CO that I would go in more massively after that I withdrew on OP Charlie, he said -- he told me to stay in place, and he was negotiating with Naser Oric. So they took it up with us, but I understand now that he asked for instructions at his higher echelon as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this caution and recommendation. At your level and at the level of your commander, did you manage to solve this problem?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not a part in that negotiation, because I was isolated on OP Charlie, of course, but my CO succeeded in the end to get the freedom of movement for the blocked patrols, and the end of the story was that the freedom of movement in the Bandera Triangle, that is what is referred to in your document as the area Podgaj-Suceska, was not restored. And as I told you yesterday, during that negotiations UN withdrew his order to restore that freedom of movement. So we were back at the status quo before the patrol started.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what do you mean when you say the "United Nations"? Are you referring to your superior commander or maybe some higher echelons?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to higher echelons. And I'll try to define that: In this case that was directly Sarajevo who was interfering, but normally our next higher echelon was the HQ of Sector North-east in Tuzla, but the -- Sarajevo oftenly took over from the Sector North-east decisions and guidelines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were told not to enter the triangle anymore, can you tell the Chamber who took this decision and who it was that was entitled to order UNPROFOR not to carry out all its duties within the area that they were deployed for the purpose of controlling the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understood it, that decision was taken on high level, but then again I don't know. I suppose that it was in Sarajevo that they accepted the lack of freedom of movement in that angle. And if your question is who was entitled to order UNPROFOR, in fact, nobody. Only UNPROFOR itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to ask your superiors when they appear here. Yesterday, you mentioned that you were unable to enter houses and other premises to seize weapons because in such instances you had to seek assistance from the police. Can you describe in more detail to the Chamber how all this was carried out?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try to make it a short story. We had patrols in the area and we discovered armed men. We tried to stop them and confiscate their weapons. In a couple of cases that we succeeded, but when they were succeeding in entering a house, we were not allowed to enter that house. That were guidelines from the UN, and then again I'm probably referring to Sarajevo. So we blocked a house like that. Then we had to call in, and that means to send a car to Srebrenica, pick up some local police who came to the house, then entered the house, searched it for weapons, I was witness at two of these events, came out and reported, "We couldn't find anything." So when that happened again and again, we in fact more or less stopped pursuing armed patrols when they were in the neighbourhood of houses 'cause that was their tactic every time, and the local police never found anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us, did you reach that agreement with the local authorities or with the OG Srebrenica command, or did you receive instructions from your higher command to act in that manner when you were searching for weapons?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we did not have any agreement on that subject, being demilitarising personnel, with local authorities or the 8th OG. We did not receive instructions. We reported that to our higher echelon, and, well, they took it for granted more or less in a way when -- when it is impossible, yeah, okay, it's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have information about the arrival of weapons for that period, 1995, when you were down there, how weapons and ammunition were coming in to the area under your control? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I recollect correctly, somewhere in April and May we saw in the distance armed men, and our patrols reported that there were new weapons. The problem was that if a patrol -- an ABiH patrol armed was about 4 or 500 metres away, we could only pursue them by foot and they ran just as hard, as fast as we could so that was quite a problem. If we had vehicles, we probably could have blocked them from entering houses and we could have done our job better. That's the only sign or the only report to which we concluded that obviously there had been some new weaponry in the enclave. And sorry, how they came in we could only guess. It could be pony express or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have on e-court Exhibit 1D31, page 1 both in English and in Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please don't remove this document from the screen. Judge Mindua has a question related to this document first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Thank you, Your Honour. I do have a question to put to the Defence. The document which is currently on the screen, 1D30, dated the 28th of January, 1995, is not signed. Do you have an explanation to give us and why this document is not signed, and what is the source of this document? This is an extremely important document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mindua -- could the document be moved slightly left on our screens so we can see the upper right-hand corner of that document, and then I'll answer your question after that's been done. Thank you. We received the document from the database of the Prosecution, of the OTP, and the number is DA17-2418 there, so I can't tell you, because the document took over -- the Defence took over that document from the database of the OTP. Thank you. And it's probably not signed because this is an incoming document being sent by Paket radio link from Srebrenica to the centre, where it says "Command Kakanj-Tuzla." So they got it from Tuzla and Kakanj, and that's why they don't -- it doesn't have a signature, because you can't send a signature through Paket link or encoded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir. You were asking for another document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Mr. President. I was asking for document ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, 1D31.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We have the document in both languages on our screens. This is an order written -- or, rather, it's an interim report of the 13th of July, 1995, sent to the 1st Corps command and forwarded to the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Izetbegovic, and it was sent by the intelligence administration from Sarajevo, the department for electronic counter-measures section, et cetera, and I'm going to read the contents. "Dear Mr. President," it says. "In view of the situation of our enclaves during the preceding period, the army General Staff has undertaken a series of military activities and procedures to organise the members of the army in the enclaves and prepare them for possible developments, primarily the defence of the existing free territory and planned engagement and preparations for future joint operations and planned operations. "Specifically, the following has been done for Srebrenica and Zepa." And then he goes on to list what has been done. "To start with, lethal assets and materiel and technical equipment were brought in on foot in fairly small quantities." That's the first bullet point. Secondly: "Seventeen helicopter sorties were carried out, in each of which a helicopter was hit. "We sent another helicopter with engineers and mechanics for one of the helicopters that was shot and had remained in Zepa and repaired it successfully, and they both -- both helicopters, returned successfully. The last sortie, unfortunately, ended tragically with the helicopter coming down near Zepa heliport, where we lost the crew of the helicopter, nine passengers and the helicopter itself. Among the passengers of the four physicians killed, three were specialists. "That is how in this way we brought back a number of seriously wounded and brought in and took back 15 from Srebrenica and five from Zepa, men who had graduated from the Officers' War College. "In preparations for future operation --" let me repeat. "In preparation for a future operation to link up the enclaves, we brought in and took back four brigade commanders, two brigade chiefs of staff, and the 26th Division Chief of Staff. The division commander who was meant to go on the next helicopter flight did not return. "After the final flight ended tragically, Naser remained."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you. Your procedure to read the whole document is very time-consuming. Is there perhaps another procedure which would shorten taking note of such a document? If perhaps you indicate which passage is relevant and then the witness could read it in a shorter way, because it is not necessary to have every document as a document and again the content on the screen. It's only because of the time you will lose for your cross-examination by reading the whole document. It's more important to get answers from the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I have understood your guideline. I'd just like us to look at page 2 where the assets are listed, the technical -- the materiel and technical equipment. So could we look at the columns there, where it says "Zepa," "Srebrenica," and then "Total" in the third column. In the first seven points we can see that what was coming in -- that weapons were coming into Srebrenica and Zepa. May we see the whole of that document on page 3 of the English so that the witness can see everything listed. So the first column is Zepa, the second is Srebrenica, and the third is the total. And can we also have page 4 displayed, the last page where we can see the signature. There's the signature. "Commander, army General Rasim Delic." Of course there's no signature there because the document was sent out in encrypted form from the Main Staff of Srebrenica, and they did not have any other means of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, my question to you is this: Does it follow from this document that weapons did come in to Srebrenica where you exerted control? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see here is an amount of ammunition, et cetera, which is said to be brought to the enclave of Srebrenica. So yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, since the army commander is informing the head of state that what we've just said -- seen, all this list, arrived in Srebrenica and Zepa, could you tell us how this materiel came into Zepa in the first place, and could that many weapons have been transported by an individual or must it have been an organised form of supply? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me how the materiel came into Zepa. Well, I really don't know because I was in Srebrenica and did not have contact or any information from Zepa. And if these are the real amounts that were resupplied, you can't do that. You have to organise it. It's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I said "Zepa," but I omitted to add the word "Srebrenica." But you saw that there were two columns, Zepa and Srebrenica, which means that it arrived in both places, more to Srebrenica than to Zepa because they probably had more need of it. Thank you. My next question is this, but --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, I'd like to have document 1D129 displayed, please. Thank you. Thank you. This is the wrong document, but anyway, to save time we'll make use of it. Well, actually, we have the right document on our screens now, and this is the first page of it. Final analysis of the Srebrenica and Zepa air-lift, and this analysis was carried out on the 17th of February, 1996, that's the date of it, in Zenica. I apologise. It's the 17th of February, 1995, not 6. And this was later in the -- in the communications centre where the date is different. May we have page 2 of this document displayed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, we should -- can't do it. In the original version we have two different years on the first page, 1996, in the heading of that page, and 1995 below this line. Both 17th of February. And we have the same in the English translation. Perhaps there is just a typo, but you could clarify that perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Most probably this document went to the communications centre of the command headquarters in Kakanj, where the people carrying out the intercepts and the department for analysis were -- it reached them. So they might have put 1996 instead of 1995, but we see that this was carried out on the 17th of February, 1995, and that it was strictly confidential under the following number, from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was compiled by the representative of the commander, Colonel Edin Hrustic, Edin Hrustic. And when we turn to page 2, we shall see that it says there: "Between the 27th of February, 1993, and the 7th of May, 1995, from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina there was an air-lift to meet the needs of the enclave of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde." And now the third line: "The main aim of introducing and maintaining the air-lift was to transport and ensure combat equipment and the evacuation of the wounded." I'm not going to quote from the document anymore. So may we now please have page 7 of this document called up. Thank you. And we see at the bottom down there -- or, rather, under (B), the penultimate paragraph, it says: 10.025 hours of flight, 10.25; GMI fuel, use approximately 8.000, et cetera, transported to Zepa UBS 17 tonnes, [indiscernible] from Zepa, 46 passengers and five wounded. So this is from Bosnia-Herzegovina to Zepa. That -- you might conclude that, but if we look at the document further down, or rather, on page -- let me just take a moment to find the page so that you can all see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Just a couple of observations about the document. The first is, I think we have an answer as to whether this document was created in 1995 or 1996 based on the first page we just saw, which described the air-lift operation lasting through May of 1995. So I hope the record's clear that we're not talking about a document from 1995 but one that was created after the fall of Srebrenica sometime in 1996 as part of an assessment of -- of what happened. I also note that the hours of flight, as I read it, is 10.25, not a thousand hours of flight as the General suggested or at least was interpreted on our LiveNote. Thirdly, I don't know if there is a supplemental Defence exhibit list for this witness, but I think this is about the fifth document in a row which we've seen which is not on the list that we received. It's not a big deal. We can follow along, but if there is a list, we'd appreciate having it so that we know what's coming down the line. I like to work with hard copies myself. It's a little bit more difficult to see one page at a time. So if there is a supplemental list, we'd appreciate getting that because we haven't had any notice of the last four or five documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber is in the same position. I didn't find these documents we have seen on the screen in your Defence list of exhibits, and therefore we are a little bit lost as well. We would appreciate to be informed in time about the exhibits you will use with the witness. Now please carry on, and indeed, we made the same observation about the time covered by this document until May 1995. Please carry on. Especially put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For the record, this -- let me say that this record was obtained from the database of the OTP and we took it over as such, and so I'm now asking questions on the basis of what we see here. So on page 7, I said that the hours of flight was 10.25 hours. The fuel consumed about 8 tonnes, 200 litres, and that it was transport -- and that to Zepa there were 7 tonnes of lethal weapons transported. I apologise if I misspoke. Now may we turn to page 10. The ERN number is 10 -- 10185442. It says here: "Attachment 1, Flights to Srebrenica." And now in the final analysis it says, on the 17th of October, [indiscernible] in flight, it says transported outgoing and incoming, lethal weapons, so many tonnes and then 20 tonnes below that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we can't follow your citation because we don't have such a date, 17th of October, on the screen. You should have a look on the screen yourself to find out if this is the right document or right page number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's why I read out the ERN number of the page. 01854422 is the number. And I read it from the document that we were provided with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: On the left side on the screen, but there is no date of October.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we look at page 9 of the English, then, please. Thank you. It says: "Attachment number 1, Flights to Srebrenica." And it is enough for us to look at the lower column where it says that lethal weapons were transported, 10 outgoing, and then 20 tonnes underneath that. So 10 and 20 tonnes. The last column. And on the way back, 10 tonnes, 20 wounded, and 29 passengers. The total that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, my question on the basis of that is as follows: Do you know -- are you aware this was -- that this was transported to Srebrenica as it says in this attachment number 1 relating to materiel going into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I am aware of is that -- sorry, we -- I described that before. On one occasion we got a report from Mike, and as I recollect, we had couple of times, two or three times, reports of overflying helicopters, but of course, I was not -- at least I did not know what was in the helicopter, even not if it landed and if where. One occasion we suspected that to have landed east of Slatina, but I described to you that before. Problem again was we had to do approaches like that by foot. If we had vehicles, we could have been quick and perhaps see or establish what happened with that helicopter, but if you try to walk about 5, 6 miles through hilly territory and you try to find a helicopter just unloading and flying away, that is impossible because you're about two hours with full equipment on your way to get to the possible spot where the helicopter landed, and then the bloody thing is gone already, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Tolimir was asking you about attachment 1. The dates I see are from the 27th of February, 1993, through the 30th of March, 1993. Can you explain anything about this time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About -- sorry, Your Honour? I did not see that, bit stupid, but no, about the period 1993, of course, I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So here we see the final analysis of flights resupplying the enclaves, carrying lethal weapons, and we have the number of tonnes, whenever the equipment was brought in. And finally I just said and I asked you to answer this: Is it possible that part of the flights, the 17 that we read out earlier on, from Zepa, were bringing in materiel from the federation to Zepa and that later on it was transported by convoy to Sarajevo precisely where you were forbidden movement; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm a bit puzzled now. Probably you mean that materiel was brought to Zepa by helicopter and then by convoy on the ground to Srebrenica, because you said Sarajevo. And then you asked me would it have been possible that it came in the enclave through the Bandera Triangle. Yes, it is possible, because as I stated before, I did not have any control over the area called Bandera Triangle. So what happened there and what the possibilities were, I can't -- can't deny that it would have been possible. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me on that point. You're quite right. Did the helicopters come from the federation to Zepa and then from Zepa, by convoy, lethal weapons taken to Srebrenica. I misspoke if I said Sarajevo. I meant Srebrenica. You said it was possible, because you weren't able to control the area. So thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd now like to ask the Presiding Judge to admit these documents, 1D30, 1D32, 1D31, and the last document that we're looking at now, that's on our screens, which was the final analysis, and it was 1D129, which was marked for identification. It was MFI'd as D63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's correct. It was identified -- marked for identification because the previous witness couldn't say anything about its content and source. Don't you think that we are in the same position now, because this witness is not able to say anything about this content of the time period February and March 1993? I don't see a background for now tendering and admitting this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please look at page number 10 in English, because you didn't allow me to show the whole document to the witness. But before that, can you please look at page 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To make it very clear, Mr. Tolimir, you say I didn't allow you to show the whole document. Of course you are in the position, you have the right to show a document, the whole document, to the witness. I was giving guidance not to read the whole document because it's time-consuming and you will lose your time for cross-examination. Just to make that very clear. Let's have that page, yes, page 10 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- and the corresponding page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the next page in B/C/S, number 11, and the number 10 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see here from this survey that the air-lift was in operation in 1995 as well. We have 31st of December, 1994; 11th of January, 1995; 6th February, 1995; 11th February 1995; 19th of April, 1995; 21st of April, 1995; 30th of April, 1995; and 7th of May, 1995. And if we turn to next page and so on and so forth, we can see what happened afterwards, but I think this will be sufficient to demonstrate that the air-lift was in operation while the witness was there. That's why I asked him this question, was it possible that helicopters provided supplies to Zepa and then that convoys carried them to Srebrenica through the Bandera Triangle from which they were banned from carrying out control. And that was the reason why I wanted this document to be tendered into evidence as an illustration of the activities that were taking place in the zone. It's not my fault that they were unable to control everything. All he said was they did notice something going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You repeated your question, but there is a certain omission. You didn't repeat the answer of the witness. The witness told us that he doesn't know anything about that and therefore he can't deny that it is possible, but I didn't hear that he has any personal knowledge about that. Could you tell us what is your personal knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we are referring to the possible move by foot from Zepa into the Bandera Triangle in order to bring in ammo -- sorry, ammunition or weapons, I wouldn't know. The question was, is that possible or would that have been possible, and that is where I said yes, it would have been possible. But do I not have knowledge of actual weapon transports in the period I was in Srebrenica through the Bandera Triangle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And therefore again, Mr. Tolimir, what is the basis of your move to admit this document through this witness? You should choose another occasion to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't need to enter this document into evidence at all. I cannot get anyone from the air force to confirm that, but the witness said that he was able to see helicopters. He also saw armed groups of men who would flee to houses whenever they were spotted. I only asked him about the supplies arriving in the enclave, and I asserted that there was a particular area in the enclave that was off limits for this witness, and it should have been controlled under the agreement. This is all I was asking for, but it's up to you to decide. It's all the same to me. But I think it's in the interests of all of us involved, including the witness, to arrive at the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, what is the position of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position of the Prosecution remains the same. This issue is not in dispute. It has never been in dispute. I can tell the Trial Chamber that if -- if General Tolimir wishes to offer this document and any similar document in a bar table motion, for example, the Prosecution will have absolutely no objection to that. As I stated a couple of days ago when we saw a similar document concerning the helicopter air-lift, this is wasting time to go over and over this material which is not in contest in this case, at least as far as the Prosecution is concerned. We don't have an objection to the document coming in today, tomorrow, yesterday, or any other day. We -- we just don't care about it that much, because it is not in contest. Again, as Your Honour has pointed out, it is General Tolimir's decision how to conduct his cross-examination, but I'm appealing on behalf of this witness and future witnesses that we are wasting time. We just spent 45 minutes on this issue. He has received the answer that he has received, and again perhaps this is best addressed in a bar table motion or something to that effect, and again we have no objection to this or similar documents. It's not an issue that weapons were coming in. They were coming in by helicopter, they were coming in by pony, they were coming in on foot to both enclaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Document D63, marked for identification, will now be admitted as an exhibit, D63. Could we have the other two documents or even three, 1D31. It's for us a problem not to have your move for tendering them at the time it is on the screen. So that we should have them back. 1D31, and then we can make a decision.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can you please not remove the document until I've finished my questions. Thank you, Mr. Thayer, and I'm grateful to the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we have now to deal with your request to admit the other documents, and we shall do that now. Otherwise, we forget about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had moved for three documents to be admitted that we had previously on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now -- yes, wait, please. Wait, please. Now I would like to have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now, please, 1D31. This one will be received, but we take into account that there are some problems with the date, but it is referring to the time until May 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D31 will be Exhibit D67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the third one was, if I remember correctly 1D32. Let's have it on the screen again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is already in evidence as Exhibit D16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have received your -- the documents you tendered. Please carry on now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please now -- D63 that we had on our screens a moment ago, and that -- I'd like to look at page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the number of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5. Thank you. Thank you. We see page 5 in Serbian. Can we have the corresponding page in English, please. That's most probably page 6. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see here note in English, which reads: "The air-lift to Zepa was also used to supply the Srebrenica zone and can be considered as an extension of the air-lift for Srebrenica." Thank you. My question is the following: Since this is indicated in the final analysis prepared by the ABiH army, the president of the War Presidency, can you tell us how it was possible that this should have been considered as an extension of the air-lift from Zepa to Srebrenica? How was it possible for it to be used for a continuation of providing supplies to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it that I, in fact, answered that before and that was when you asked me to the possibility that air-lift operations into Zepa with supplies for Srebrenica and then by foot coming in to Srebrenica, and then I said that that would have been possible, especially through the Bandera Triangle, because that was an area which I did not control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us was there a land corridor connecting Zepa and Srebrenica and you were in the latter enclave? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean with a land corridor? There was a land -- sorry, could you tell me what you mean with a land corridor. Of course there was land. There was normal terrain between Zepa and Srebrenica. If you mean, "Did you know about a certain route they took?" Well, I answered that before. I do not, and the only thing is that we had once or twice contact with a pony express coming into the enclave in the south, and I pointed out on the map that that was the reason we established OP Kilo and OP Delta. I wanted another one but that wasn't possible because we didn't have the material. Is that an answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You have answered my question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document D61, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before this document will be removed, Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Actually it's a clarification. What is a pony express?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I -- and I understand your question. We discovered that the ABiH or arranged by the opstina, the civil so-called government of the enclave, there was more or less regularly a kind of supply convoy in the direction of Zepa and then after they -- it came back, and they used ponies to carry the load they had. So we called that the pony express. I hope that answers your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. It does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see document D61 on our screens, and can you please look at paragraph 3. I'm going to quote only portion of it. The division command issued a strictly confidential order 01-33/95, on 18th of May, 1995, to the units that belonged to it. They were ordered to carry out specific combat tasks in the corridor between Srebrenica and Zepa. According to this order, the 282nd Mountain Light Brigade, the 283rd, also Mountain Light Brigade, and the 285th Light Mountain Brigade shall carry out daily reconnaissance and patrol activities in the corridor in order to protect the corridor from being intersected by the aggressor. This will be carried out by armed patrols. This order was drafted by the commander or the Chief of Staff, Ramiz Becirevic, who took over the duty of commander on the 27th of May, 1995, and he sent it the command of the 285th Zepa Brigade. My question is: Was the Zepa Brigade securing this corridor as far as the Bandera Triangle, and from then on it was taken over by the units from Srebrenica? Although you didn't have access to this triangle, do you know in what way this triangle was secured? And I'm asking for your opinion as an expert in these matters.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know whether the Zepa Brigade was securing any corridor because I had no contact with that. I take it that that brigade was stationed in the Zepa enclave. Again, again you say, asking my opinion as an expert, that they would come in with that, with contraband and weapons, et cetera, in the Bandera Triangle. As an expert, I take that highly not impossible but not very likeable because our OP Charlie and the VRS positions were very close together in that area. We had line of sight in a small valley, and that meant that those transport had to pass that valley. Unless they came from the south, as I pointed out, one on the many routes in the south, directly north of that mining area, and entered there the Bandera Triangle out of southern direction, which, as an expert, I think is more possible and -- and stop -- is a better possibility. Whether units from the 28th Division took over securing a corridor, I do not know. Problem is that we found out that they -- when they moved out or in, they did that by night, and it was, by the UN and then again probably Sarajevo, forbidden to us to operate in patrols by night. We had to stay home. So I can't answer that in the sense that I do not know of units of the 28th Division securing any corridor between Zepa and Srebrenica in the area you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you don't know that that was maintained during the daylight while you were on the ground, but as I said, do you know if that was going on during the night as well? And if necessary, I can show you the map again.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know the map so that wouldn't be necessary. Sure it was maintained during the daylight, but we had no access to Serb territory, and the -- mentioned by you, corridor to Zepa was for us in Serb territory. So the only thing we could see was the line of sight out of our OPs or what our patrols saw -- said. And in the south it is a very hilly territory, you know, so my line of sight was very short. So if they were there in that area, I wouldn't have noticed as long as there was no fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But why do you say that that was the Serb territory of Zepa, because it was the Muslims who were passing through this area trading goods and doing all other kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then you misunderstood me. I meant to say that the area between the enclave of Srebrenica and the enclave of Zepa was Bosnian Serb territory. We were not allowed to patrol in that area, as you know. So that's why I said when they were busy there and did not actually have fire contact, I wouldn't know because I couldn't see. I could not observe that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand what you told us about what you were capable of doing. I think that with this we have concluded the discussion about these two subjects. Now we are going to move to another topic with which you are familiar. So we have finished with the subject of the supplies coming into the demilitarised areas. And we are going to conclude the subject of air-lift supplies of weapons for Srebrenica and Zepa. Can you tell me are you aware that the Main Staff was sending to UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo protest letters because of the helicopter flights that were going on, and against providing supplies to these zones, and I'm talking about the year of 1995, while you were there.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it that you mean with the Main Staff, the Main Staff of the VRS, and I am not aware or was not informed that protests like that were sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, you were never told from Sarajevo about the reasons that the VRS was alleging that these zones were not demilitarised and why they were putting up ultimatums that they were going to secure demilitarisation of these zones themselves. So you are saying that you know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Just -- I have to add something, sorry. In the -- I take it it was the 10th or 11th of July, there was an ultimatum from the -- to the -- sorry, from the VRS to DutchBat which started with the verb: "You did not demilitarise the zone, so we are taking up that," but that's the only time I was confronted with these words and they came not from UN Sarajevo. They came from the VRS, by radio, during the end phase, so to say, in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, do you believe that combat operations were conducting there precisely by the army of the VRS in order to separate these two enclaves? Can you also tell us in what way did you receive information from your command regarding reactions from the parties involved?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to be sure that I understand the question well, which period do you mean that these actions by the army or operations, combat operations, by the VRS in order to separate those two enclaves? Do you refer to the period before the end of attack or do you refer to the attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please answer the second part of my question. In what way did you receive information about the response by the parties involved to the activities in the zones under your control? And I'm talking about the protests that were being sent to your command in Sarajevo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I told you that I didn't know about the protests, so I was not informed by my higher echelon, the UN, about protests. And as a consequence, I did not know what measures they took. If the question goes that far that you ask, "Did you get special guidelines about the contents of protests," no, but again, I didn't hear about those protests. Exchanged between Main Staff and UN Sarajevo, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you tell us whether the Dutch Battalion had information about the fact that there was an imminent attack against the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, no. We got a report -- the only thing that pointed in that direction was a report by UNHCR who came in pretty nervously with a convoy and told us that they saw three Tango 55s and some artillery moving along the road with amount of troops. And that's the only thing I knew or, say, more or less warning I got. We didn't get that far that, as a consequence of the movement of three main battle tanks and some artillery, we did not conclude that there was an attack imminent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that you didn't have a plan, or perhaps you did have a plan, in case there were to be an attack against the enclave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a plan but not triggered by -- by any events. Pretty early we already made a plan where, for instance, the blocking positions Bravo A1 till 4, we'll speak of that, I suppose, later, were reccy'd and planned but that's about it. Oh, no, there was a blocking position planned at the north side, say, just north of the HQ of the DutchBat in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have on e-court D20, page 17, paragraph 248. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think this could be a convenient time for the first break before we move to the next document. If you agree, we should have the first break now, but before we do that, I have to correct myself. My comment on different dates, on page 26, lines 9 to 10 was related to document D67, but that was a mistake. It -- the problem with the dates was in the document D63. We have our first break now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I asked for a document on e-court. D20 was the number, page 17, paragraph 2.48. It's a report on Srebrenica based on debriefing conducted in Assen in 1995. And there we have the paragraph, 2.48, and this is what it says: "The commander of the Dutch Battalion assumed that the BiH forces in the event of a large BiH offensive would try, when DutchBat left the observation posts, to confiscate weapons and vehicles with the use of force if necessary. He expressly requested the BH Army in the enclave, after the aforementioned loss of the observation post, for sufficient freedom of movement to be -- to implement DutchBat's operation plan in the event of a BSA offensive. The plan consisted of falling back to blocking positions which were to seal off the access roads to the towns of Srebrenica and Potocari. These blocking positions, incidentally, were only able to discourage the BSA and had scarcely any military import as the white infantry fighting vehicles stood virtually in the middle of the road without any other form of protection. "Apart from an arrangement that the BiH would occupy positions between the observation posts, no co-ordination took place between DutchBat and the BiH regarding the response in the event of an offensive by the BSA. The aforementioned arrangement was to prevent the BiH from taking up a position immediately in front of or behind an observation post, thus attracting BSA fire and endangering the observation post."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, my question to you is this: From what we've just read out, from this paragraph, we can see that there was an operation plan on the part of the DutchBat if there were to be a BSA attack on the enclave. Can you tell us when this plan came into being, what period of time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I -- as I stated before, that would have been made somewhere around March. Not with the direct cause but just what you do is, in a situation like that, being a soldier, you look for eventualities and try to prepare a response on that. And in that sense, one of the eventualities was an attack by the VRS, and that's why we -- did -- sorry, did reconnaissance, the positions Bravo 1 till 4 and a position north of the HQ as mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please tell us now whether during the attack by the Army of Republika Srpska in Srebrenica, whether that UNPROFOR operative plan was put into effect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, it was. At least we tried, but due to hostile fire we had to adjust some positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us now whether you had any knowledge or tell us about what you knew then between the clashes between Muslim armed formations amongst themselves, what you knew about that and if you did, and whether there was any mention of that during the debriefings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your first question, yes, I was aware, and I knew there were clashes between Muslim armed formations and the VRS. OPs reported to me battle noise in different -- in several areas. Personally, we could report or see artillery impacts, artillery firing, mortar firing. That was mentioned, as far as I know, during the debriefings, if you mean the debriefings that took place in Holland afterwards, after we returned from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have page 38 displayed, please, of this same exhibit, D20, that we see on our screens. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before we deal with the next paragraph, just tell me this: The UNPROFOR command, with whom did it reach an agreement about this plan to block the axes of attack from the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean by the UNPROFOR command, the staff in Sarajevo, I don't have a clue. And I doubt whether there was an agreement with anybody, because it was a battalion plan, and just in the -- in the course of what we call contingency planning. You -- as I said, you considered possibilities or possible events and tried to plan and make a reaction on that, whether they come, these events really will occur or not, that's a normal military procedure. And again to be clear, in that period I was, in fact, on an island, away from any information or very little information. So my -- my helicopter view, so to say, was very limited, limited to the area of Srebrenica, and I don't have any idea what UNPROFOR staffs discussed with whoever, VRS or even BiH. I was not informed about that. So again, it was contingency planning, and there was not an agreement with anybody about that. It was an order within the battalion, and I don't have the custom of discussing that with half the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I quoted the last portion of the paragraph we looked at a moment ago, and I needed that for me to be able to ask my question, and I'd like to repeat the following sentences: Except for the arrangement for the BH Army to take up positions between the observation posts, between the DutchBat and the BH Army there was no co-ordination. So did I understand this correctly? Was there an agreement whereby they would occupy positions, and if so, who was the agreement reached between, because that's what this seems to refer to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an agreement that they would take positions between the OPs, and the agreement was between me, being the DCO of DutchBat by consent of the CO, of course, and the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, Mr. Ramiz.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It says here that there was no longer any co-ordination as far as possible attacks against the enclaves existed, that there was no co-ordination with the Muslims. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing we agreed upon was that in case of that attack, they would take positions between our OPs, our observation posts, and the very moment they would leave their positions they would inform the local OP commander. That's all. Further co-ordination didn't take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have on e-court 1D29. Thank you. Thank you. We can see it now. This is an order of the 4th of June, 1995, that is to say, a month before the events we're talking about took place, written by -- or signed by corps command -- the corps commander and sent to Srebrenica to the 28th Division, and I'm going to read its contents out. "I hereby command," point 1 -- "I hereby order: "Occupy the unoccupied and abandoned Dutch Battalion observation posts with our forces and establish defence lines behind them on the same level facing the aggressor forces." So that is linked to your observation post. Now: "2. Monitor the Dutch-controlled observation posts and organise elements of defence, combat formation, behind them in order to eliminate potential negative consequences which might arise should the aggressor take control of the observation posts. "3. Continuously monitor the activities of the aggressor and the Dutch Battalion and immediately inform the 2nd Corps Command of any changes or new intelligence. "5. The tasks shall be carried out immediately ..." And the signature is Commander Brigadier Sead Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, my question is this: Did you know, were you aware of the fact that the agreement you had was in part contained in this order on taking over your positions and observation posts by the BH Army? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware that they had ordered to occupy abandoned Dutch observation posts, but in that time, the only observation post that was abandoned or was taken over by the VRS was, in fact, Echo, because the day before Echo fell. More or less the agreement I had with the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division is contained in this order. There's just one annoying detail that he orders them to take positions behind us while we co-ordinated they would have the positions on our flanks, so in the same line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the second line of this point it says: "To set up a defence line behind or in the same line with -- on the same level facing the aggressor forces," at the level of your observation posts. Can you see that that is what it says there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender document 1D29. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D68.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber now if, on the same level as you you have the BH Army forces, can the Army of Republika Srpska, at the time of the attack, differentiate between you and members of the BH Army; and how would it know what your intentions were and what the BH Army's intention were? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could differentiate because there it was obvious that we were just confined to the location of the OP and that was obvious what was OP and not. I described to you before that they were painted white, et cetera, and open and bare. The trenches of the ABiH were not exactly next to the OPs. There was always a space about 20, 50 metres, and sometimes they were behind us. So I don't think it would be -- it would have been a big problem to see what is ABiH and what is an OP. Whether they were aware of our intentions, as far as I know, the VRS knew that we would defend our OP in case of an attack. I suppose that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just tell us, for the purposes of Trial Chamber and the record, whether BH Army members were on the same level or same defence line with your observation posts according to the plan that was compiled in March, as early as March.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That co-ordination about being in line with us was later than March, and March was our contingency plan for the blocking positions, just for the record. On some spots they were on the same line, but for instance, Echo and Foxtrot, they were not in the same line and not even within 100 metres of the OP. Echo, there was BiH position on the high grounds directly left of the OP. But then again, the ABiH fought out of trenches and we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you this in view of the fact that your operations plan provided for you to be in the middle.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, may we have 1D20 once again on our screens, please. Paragraph 13. It's page 46 of this debriefing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the paragraph number be repeated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, this is D20.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You have -- you have been able to read this. I'll read it for the record. "At 15 metres from -- BiH soldiers complete with blue caps or blue hats came within a distance of 15 metres from one of the observation posts. Resembling UN personnel, they opened fire from the position in the direction of the BCA [as interpreted] front line so that it seemed as if the UN had opened fire. In this way, they attempted to draw fire from the BSA on the observation post and thus involve DutchBat in the combat actions." So this is from the debriefing report. Could you now tell us whether you have information on what observation post this is here. Which one does it refer to, for the record? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. First the period was before, as far as I can see, because I can't see that the contacts are not -- this is not given a time or a period that it happened, but I think it refers to some incidents that happened mostly at OP Alpha where, before the attack, the ABiH some -- at some occasions did this trick. I was witness of one -- one time that it happened. But as far as I know, this was before the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us roughly how many days before or was it during combat action? Why would they do this if there wasn't any combat action? There must have been some combat situation. Can you remember anything about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your first question how many days, well, incidents like this happened in April and May, and the incident I described at OP Alpha would have been end of April, probably, but then again I do not remember the exact date. And why they did that, I don't know. Probably to -- to bring DutchBat in a bad position towards the VRS or what, but that is guessing. I don't know. Ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you to tell us whether there were persistent endeavours on the part of the BH Army in Srebrenica to involve UNPROFOR, as you said a moment ago, in the conflict with the Army of Republika Srpska. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the endeavours they did were creating incidents like this, and there was not a pattern. It happened once in awhile, but there was not a clear pattern as far as the location where it happened or the period or the amount of incidents. It was random.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since in battle death can occur within moments, can you tell us what you did to prevent this from happening, and did you take any steps to prevent it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, we protested at the staff of the 28th Division with, as far as I could see, no result. In the case I was witness of an incident like that, I had one of my machine-guns open overhead fired from a flank and they ran away. The VRS did not respond on that, because probably they could see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have page 2478 displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Or, rather, I'd like to draw your attention to what I'm going to read out from page 278 from the Popovic trial, lines 19 to 23, and I'm going to quote what you said there in the transcript. "Foxtrot -- after the Foxtrot incident -- or, rather, the killing [Realtime transcript read in error "willing"] of one of my soldiers, we ordered the observation posts to -- and positions to withdraw only when given permission to do so. Only if there were some sort of agreement reached with the local Muslim commanders, because we wished to prevent any more soldiers being shot by the Bosnian Army."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there is a correction needed in the transcript on page 42, line 23, the first word should read "killing" instead of "willing." Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was this: When this was going on -- or, rather, when did this happen? Was it before or after the green order had been given?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before the green order had been given. Yes, the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, a moment ago, in that quotation I read out, you said that some sort of agreement with the -- you mentioned some sort of agreement with the local Muslims. Did you mean to say that you had co-ordination with them, that you co-ordinated your activities with theirs, and didn't you think that that might be suspect, this co-ordination of activities in the field? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I meant to say exactly what I said. After the event of the killing of one of my soldiers and immediately -- having experience with lack of discipline of commanders, local commanders, to obey orders from the 28th Division, I gave that order to the OP commander that if he, on that spot, on that very moment, could co-ordinate with the local BiH commander that he was starting to move, that was one of the conditions that he could get permission to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The transcript says, "this is one of the positions," the "positions" must be "conditions."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if this movement on the battle-field between you and the Muslims, if you are advancing, they're advancing, and vice versa, could be perceived as if you were conducting a joint action against the VRS and that the VRS was actually your target?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First a remark. The question is not advancing but withdrawing, and, of course, it could have been seen as a joint action, and in case of an attack by the VRS, don't let that be any misunderstanding, the VRS was our target.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us this: When this soldier of yours was killed by the Muslims, how far was the killer from him? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 3, 4 metres, as was reported to me. It happened when they crossed the obstacles the Muslim forces had laid on that road, and the Muslim soldiers were quite close next -- or standing at that barrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please now look at paragraph 4.14. Thank you. It reads as follows: "It also transpired that the BiH soldiers were not always recognisable as military personnel. Men who had previously been seen in uniform fighting in the southern section of the enclave were recognised by DutchBat personnel, when the former had mingled, in civilian clothing, among the refugees moving from Srebrenica to Potocari or when they were on the compound in Potocari. Local women, known to be members of the BiH, were also seen later in civilian clothing." Thank you. Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber what kind of difficulties you encountered because these individuals appeared in your vicinity in civilian clothing, including women who were members of the BH Army and who also appeared attired as civilians? Can you tell us something more about this situation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, simply it is what the -- what the document says. I was reported by soldiers of B Company that men they saw before fighting the VRS, they recognise -- in partial uniforms, they recognised them in -- when the civilian people came to Potocari, they recognised them in the crowd. Then they were in civilian. And as far as the women are concerned, as I remember well, it concerned two young women who were seen in uniform before and later on when, well, Srebrenica -- I'm sorry. When Srebrenica was -- had fallen, they were seen in civil clothes in the crowd at the bus station. So it's just what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall go back now to this event regarding co-ordination and co-operation. It is obvious that you were forced to co-ordinate and co-operate on the ground, and in that respect I would like us to look at paragraph 3.58. It's on page 38. Thank you. "On Monday, 10th of July, the commander of the OP M received orders from the C Company commander to co-ordinate with the BH. That evening, fighting broke out amongst the BiH soldiers, resulting in dead and wounded. At around noon on Tuesday, the 11th of July, a number of shells struck the area near the armoured vehicle. The abandoned OP was also shelled. Chaos prevailed among the BiH forces. Internal fighting broke out once again. "That evening, the OP crew were permitted to leave because they were willing to take the wife and children of a local BH leader with them. When the two BiH soldiers with the antitank weapons attempted to prevent their departure, they were shot in the head by the BH Army leader. This led once again to fighting between the BiH soldiers. "On the route to Potocari, they picked up many refugees. They came under fire on two more occasions. At 01.30 hours on Wednesday, the 12th of July, they arrived in Potocari where they joined the B Company positions to the south of the compound." After reading this paragraph, I will kindly ask you to tell me what you know about this fighting which resulted in the killing of your soldier and which was described in the debriefing report, based on what you know about the incident?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's exactly the text in that debriefing report. That is what I know about it. That's the same content as was reported by C Company commander to me. I have one remark. Your conclusion was that it was necessary for me to co-ordinate and co-operate on the ground. Just to be clear, that co-operation existed purely by an OP commander who saw or called the local BiH commander and said, "I want to go there. Do you agree?" That's it. So there's not a big meeting or -- just one remark or two questions of an OP commander. But again, back to your last question, I knew about this event and it was reported to me exactly as written down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
