utterances.text: Thank you. Is it then true that the C Company commander co-ordinated his activities on the battle-field and his movements in agreement and with co-ordination with members of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, again, the level of co-ordination is here the OP commander of OP Mike, and to make clear why that happened, a period preliminary to this event, the OP Mike was shelled by the VRS, and they got my permission to withdraw about 4, 500 metres to the edge of the village, as I remember well, in Jaglici. And that is where this happened, because C -- commander C Company wanted that APC on another position as it was, but then he was not allowed in the beginning by the local BiH to do so and threatened with the two antitank guns where the message speaks about. So again, here it was a co-ordination. A big word for just a question of the OP commander to the local BiH commander, "I want to move down there. Do you agree?" Or just the message that, and then you saw the reaction of the local BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This might become clear if you look at a practical example.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at P567, page 2 in English, last paragraph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's -- it's P607, P607. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please switch on your microphone, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 2. Last paragraph in English, and page 3 in Serbian, where you say as follows: "The BH members threatened to shoot at our soldiers if they left their observation post, which then happened. That was how a Dutch soldier came to be killed by the BH Army. It happened with a dumdum bullet. I believe that shooting at UN personnel with a shotgun is a war crime. It was clearly proven what kind of ammunition was used in the shooting of the soldier. I gave the X-ray pictures to the military police." This is my question: Was the Dutch Battalion exposed to threats from the BH Army, and whether they used weapons, I mean BH Army members used weapons in order to threaten lives of the UN personnel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions in the end phase where we tried to move our APCs to positions we thought were correct, and one of the situations was just described at Mike, OP Mike, we were threatened by the local BiH soldiers with mostly an antitank weapon or with light weapons. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you speak here about dumdum bullets and after that about a shotgun, are you referring here to dumdum bullets whose use was prohibited by -- by the first Hague conference, 1899, because this is the bullets that disintegrate within a human body, or are you talking about something completely different?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about dumdum bullets. And how the word "shotgun" came in, because shotgun is something else, I do not know. I got reports from my dressing station, my hospital, when van Renssen died. They made X-ray pictures, and their conclusion was that it had to be done by not normal ammunition. We looked at that and with a demolition expert, and we came to the conclusion that they used dumdum bullets. Being convinced of the fact that that should be considered as -- as a war crime, I handed the X-rays to the military police detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, because I didn't quite understand what the correlation was here, but earlier on I asked you about the green order. Now I'm asking you was it you who issued this order?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the battalion it was, but the base of that order was the order of the UN, being Sarajevo, to defend Srebrenica with all means. And translating to my level, that order, the written green order to B Company went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber whether the issuing of the green order implies that UNPROFOR soldiers simply took sides, and that is to say they took side with those who were defending Srebrenica. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take side. I was ordered as a UN unit to defend the city, and there was a party that was doing the same, of course, but we didn't take side in the literal word or meaning of those words. I had -- I could not order the means of the ABiH or anything. I had just my own means to defend the city according to the order of UN Sarajevo. And that -- we had a common enemy, common, I mean the ABiH and the UN at that time, is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that UNPROFOR and ABiH fired each from their own weapons at the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber, did the green order mean that an engagement in combat operations should be undertaken regardless of what was contained in blue, red, and other orders?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know whether I understand your question correctly, but it meant that, for instance, the rules of engagement given to us before as a UN unit, one of our problems we were only to use our weapons in self-defence, were ruled out and we went back to the rules of engagement of an army, any army, in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying this. Can you tell us now, please, were you already a legitimate target of those whose lives you threatened through these combat operations, as you described them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of the issuing of the green order, we were in combat with the VRS, and the VRS was a target for us, and in fact the opposite is -- is realistic and true as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please switch on your microphone, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You have explained this in a fair and correct way, meaning that one side is entitled to use weapons against the side threatening their lives.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now tender Prosecution document 65 ter 104.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let us know which document this is. We have another document on the screen. Are you tendering that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 104, Prosecution document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what is it about? I don't know if you have it on the screen. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant to have it on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You mean the document on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Instead of this document, can we now please have on e-court 65 ter 104. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That was perhaps a misunderstanding because you said, "I tender this document." You have it now on the screen. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We have the document here, the document which was sent to the Drina Corps -- or, rather, by the Drina Corps, on the 8th of July, to all its units that were engaged in operations in Srebrenica. It reads: "The UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo has filed a protest note with the Main Staff over operations against UNPROFOR observation point 652808 (UNPROFOR map, near Zeleni Jadar). They emphasised that their point was captured by artillery and tank action. The Main Staff of the VRS answered that the Drina Corps command had been informed that the Muslims were using six armoured personnel carriers painted white and bearing UNPROFOR markings and that the Muslims were -- had started offensive operations from Srebrenica in order to join up the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa. "The RS Main Staff demanded that UNPROFOR warn the Muslim forces to withdraw to within the borders of the demilitarised zones and stay marked on the map in accordance with the agreement, and disarm them in accordance with the agreement. The Main Staff also demanded that UNPROFOR not set up observation points outside the marked demilitarised zones. "The Main Staff has ordered you not to attack UNPROFOR but to prevent any possible surprises and stop the Muslims in their intention to link up Srebrenica with Zepa. "Good luck in war and best regards from General Tolimir." This is a telegram of the Main Staff conveyed by General Milenko Zivanovic to all units and signed by him. Can you tell us whether you were aware of the fact that the Main Staff had sent a protest note to UNPROFOR about the use by the Muslims of vehicles painted white and bearing UNPROFOR markings? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know anything about that protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you know nothing about the protest. That means that from the sector command, because our headquarters had links with your command, I assume -- well, did they convey anything to you as observations made from the Main Staff of about the -- what was going on in the area that you controlled and their conduct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean our headquarters being the Main Staff, again I did not get any information that there -- of allegedly offensive of the ABiH in the area south of the enclave, nor did I get any reports from my OPs that could indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And can you tell us whether you knew anything at all or whether any checks were carried out on your part to the effect that the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska was issuing warnings that the Muslims were using six APCs painted white?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recollect that that incident within this -- this framework. I know that in -- anywhere in April, I got a report of one of my OPs. They reported two BTR-60s, being eight-wheeled APCs, painted white, coming out of southern direction and driving into the enclave at pretty high speed. We tried to catch them but -- or to confirm that they were there, but we -- afterwards we never found them again, and during the attack we never ourselves saw that the ABiH used APCs. But this story about the, what was it, six APCs, armoured vehicles, is unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have on e-court 1D207, please. It's a document entitled "Interview with Franken," dated the 31st of March, 1999. The document exists only in English, and it was disclosed to the Defence by the Prosecution a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering the last document as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, I am tendering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now see document 1D207, please. We have it on our screens. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, since the document is in English and you were able to see what it's about, I said it was your interview, can you tell me if you remember having given that interview and, if so, to whom? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't have the faintest idea. I see here a text, probably gave that interview, but be aware of the fact that when we came back there were numerous committees, investigations, et cetera, so I do not know - I can't see it on the document as well - to whom this interview is given. I see that the tape recording failed and the text is a reconstruction of the discussed, but I'm sorry, I can't recollect to whom this was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can see the headline and the last page of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see the headline, and as far as I can see the first page until point 13.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That you. That's sufficient for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can provide some background to this document, Mr. President, and this was also clarified for the Defence when we sent it over. Pursuant to a specific request from one of the accused in the Popovic case, we undertook considerable effort to obtain various interviews from the Dutch Institute for War Documentation. You're heard references to the NIOD report. That's the acronym for the Dutch version of the name I just stated. So in connection with that specific request in the last case, we obtained various statements that were disclosed to us by NIOD. NIOD went ahead and deleted certain sections of various interviews based on their own criteria, and those interviews turned up during the course of our regular database searches in preparation for the witnesses so we turned that over. But this is a NIOD apparently conducted interview from March of 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to Mr. Thayer, and thanks to the witness, because even before I asked my question, he said that he did have some knowledge about these two transporters. I'm not going to debate the point, because he was sincere and frank in his answer. But can we take a look at paragraph 1 now, please. It says here: "The BH Army smuggled two armoured transporters, armoured cars, BTR armoured cars, into the enclave via the north." It says "north" here. "There was notified by a Dutch OP, observation post. They were never found, those two vehicles. Later it became clear that the Ukrainians in Zepa were missing a total of five. Bought or stolen by the BH Army?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I understand you. I don't even have to ask the question. What you -- I'm sure you want to say something and comment on it. Thank you, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I found out that -- that because I see that this reconstruction has some faults. For instance, smuggled them not allegedly through the north but through the south, of course. And I saw that the Ukrainian unit in Zepa, in a logistic report, because that's the kind of information we got from the UN, reported the missing of five armoured personnel carriers. And the last remark is a cynical assumption which I would not repeat in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand you, but this isn't a document introduced by the Defence. I'm just making use of it to look at certain elements necessary here for us to learn what happened. From this we can see, and you yourself say that these vehicles were never found. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were they white vehicles? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They looked like -- no looked like. They appeared to be UN vehicles. So all white and the U and N letters on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As you said that you'd seen them in Srebrenica and that they passed through at great speed --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now look at P581, please. Thank you. Thank you. We have here a note compiled by Louis Fortin on talks between General Gobillard and General Gvero. May we turn to page 2, because I'd like us to look at a paragraph there that I'm interested in, and it reads as follows. Next page, please, page 2. He claimed -- he claimed, General Gvero: "That a large number of vehicles, UN vehicles, stolen by BH troops, which were still painted white, were used against the Bosnian Serb army. He said he had no absolute knowledge of who the troops in the vehicles belonged to but drew the general's attention to the BSA reliable information that those were BH Army troops." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, from this note and from what you've already said and what we read out in that first document, do we see that General Gvero pointed to what was happening on the ground, that is to say, five vehicles disappeared. You said they appeared and that you saw two of them in Srebrenica, and that they had been painted white and had UN markings. So is it possible that those vehicles went into action, as the BSA army claims, according to General Gvero, and that we had reliable information telling us that they were BH Army forces? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, you concluded that I saw those vehicles in Srebrenica, which is incorrect. My OP only saw them entering the enclave at the south border. That is just a remark for the question before. And I didn't get exactly when, in what period or where those large number of vehicles, UN vehicles, were seen. Is that referring to the Srebrenica area or any other area? Then again, we only saw two and never saw them again, but if you ask me if anything is possible, I can confirm that. In battle, anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you were right to correct me. That's very proper of you. And when I said "you," I meant UNPROFOR, not you personally. So I'm grateful for you -- to you for pointing it out that that was an observer who saw this. But anyway, it was five vehicles which the Army of Republika Srpska noticed and told UNPROFOR about it. Now, were you ever asked to verify this, to check it out, by the UNPROFOR command after these protest notes by General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, did I not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document P581. Oh, it's already an exhibit I'm told. Thank you. So I don't need to tender it. But now may we look at an earlier document that was on e-court before this one, which was 1D207. Thank you. Thank you. We have it here again. Now, what we saw in the interview and the description of what was happening on the ground, without going into how they wrote this, that these APCs were bought or stolen from Zepa, and further down, in paragraph 6, they go on to say: "Weapons were regularly smuggled --" this is from your interview, "from Zepa straight through the Serbian lines and local BSA commanders were richly rewarded for this. Occasionally, an ABiH smuggling team ran into an ambush and several Muslim fighters were shot. But after this, the smuggling carried on as normal. Horses were sometimes used for this." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question on the basis of that is this: Did the UNPROFOR command in Srebrenica know about what you say here, that there was smuggling going on from Zepa to Srebrenica, and that that was -- that horses were used for that, horses and vehicles such as the two transporters that passed by at great speed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew about that information that we got from -- out of our personnel, and then I mean the local personnel. We had quite some locals working at our -- our camp site, at our HQ, and they were a good source for information. The horses I related to here is that so-called pony express, which I explained to Your Honour what it was. You said "vehicles." I do not know of any vehicles, especially not those BTRs, being used for smuggling. That's not what I said there as well. That probably will answer your question. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. They came from the south to the enclave, as you said. BTRs are combat vehicles; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well -- sorry. Not in the military sense of the word. BTRs are APCs, armoured personnel carriers. They're not fit to go in combat because they're too poorly armed and not armoured enough to see upon them as an infantry fighting vehicle. That is a vehicle that you can bring in fighting as well, but it is an armoured personnel carrier, yes, and there is heavy machine-gun on the top of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for that fair and correct answer. Just tell me this: Did you send out information to your superior command in Sarajevo about what was going on linked to this smuggling and the entry of these vehicles that were observed at your observation posts? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, you're talking about two events. The information we had about smuggling and once in awhile confirmed by seeing that all kind of things were offered at the black market in Srebrenica was reported to the UN. The fact that the pony express paid local BSA commanders just for -- to let them through was reported to the UN. And the second case, the two vehicles, the two BTRs, was of course reported to the UN. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You're quite right. Now, on transcript page 2438, lines 14 to 16, in the Popovic Defence case, you talk about the changes which took place in the enclaves in May 1995, and you say, I quote: "Suddenly we saw that members of the BH," Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, "wore new uniforms and new combat uniforms." Now, my question is this: Does that confirm that this was smuggled in or arrived into the enclaves in some other way? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did arrive in some way, because I was not aware that there was -- they were capable of making them themselves. So probably smuggled in or whatever. They came into the enclave, and in May we saw them walking around in combat suits.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In paragraph 7 you say the following, and I quote: "Weapons were also regularly brought into the enclave from Tuzla." And now paragraph 41. May we turn to that, please. Paragraph 41, quote -- it says that you said in your interview: "Franken is certain that there were American weapons deliveries to the BH Army. These weapons were delivered in Tuzla and transported further from there." I went on to the next question, but let me stay with my first observation. Could I have your comments to that portion of your interview to this agency?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning page [sic] 41, as I said before, they comprised themselves, the taped one again, and I am certain, as it said here, that means that I had proof for it. It is an assumption that there were weapons coming in through -- American weapons coming into the ABiH. That assumption was based on reports I got from my A Company, and our A Company was in the area of Tuzla and had a station on Tuzla, our 3rd Company as a self-supporting detachment, about lending -- what do you call them? Yeah, aircraft, but Hercules aircrafts [indiscernible] identified. Pretty shortly after that, we saw that there, as reported before, there were new Kalashnikovs in the area. So I did the assumption that that had a connection, these two, but again it is a personal opinion. It is not proven. I don't have proof of it, and I didn't have any evidence to show that did happen. In this interview, I gave an opinion and I don't know exactly what I said, but I saw other points that are absolutely not true, and that it wasn't said by us. But they lost, as I saw, the tape, and they made it themselves out of the memory. The idiocy that UNHCR, in point 40, smuggled batteries for us is in -- untrue, and I never said that, for instance. And point 41 is a personal opinion, but again an assumption, and I didn't have any proof or evidence for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now as far as this is concerned, for the Trial Chamber and these proceedings, can you give us your analysis as to how it was possible that weapons arrived from Tuzla to the enclave. How was that possible?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in fact we discussed that before, and in any way brought in, being by, on some occasions, the -- signalled by us a helicopter or through Zepa and through the south by foot. They are the most obvious possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you had any knowledge of the fact that in humanitarian convoys weapons were being brought into the enclave for the Muslims to use? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And if I would have, I would have taken them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now in paragraph 29, which we can't see on our screens at the moment, paragraph 29, your relations with Charlie Brantz were mentioned. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether you know who that man is, the one referred to in paragraph 29, Charlie Brantz. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a paragraph 29 now in front of me where the colonel Brantz is not mentioned, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. That was my mistake. Not 29 but paragraph 10. Thank you. Charlie Brantz.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Charlie Brantz, you want me to describe who he was and what my relationship with him was or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, we can narrow that question down. I'm not interested in your relation with him. All I'm interested in is what he could have had to do with Zepa and Srebrenica and the people from Zepa and Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Charlie Brantz was a colonel, a Dutch colonel, being one of the chief of staffs of the command in Sector North-east. So he was, in fact, our next higher echelon, Chief of Staff of the unit that was our next higher echelon, and because we knew each other out of Holland, former times, it was easy or easier to discuss or to speak with him than with unknown international staff. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. In the transcript it said Dutch colonel being one of the staff commands, must be Chief of Staff in Sector North-east.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Would you now take a look at paragraph 12 of your 31st of March statement, 2010. It's not very clear, so if I may, I'm going to read it out because I wasn't able to fully understand it. It is this witness's statement -- or, rather, the previous witness's statement that we quoted earlier on. P607 is the document number. In the statement you gave to the Tribunal, here's what you say: "When Franken required air support in Tuzla --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please give the page or paragraph number in English and B/C/S so that we can follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the previous document. P -- what number? 207.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was referring to P607. You asked for that. Or to 1D207.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D207. Thank you. Thank you. We have paragraph 12 on our screens now, of your 31st of March 210 [as interpreted] statement. I'll read it out and you can clarify what you meant. "When Franken requested air support in Tuzla, he got through to a Pakistani officer who repeatedly insisted that Observation Post Mike and OP Echo were not on his map. In other words, there could be no air support because the BSA could not carry out attacks on OPs which did not exist. Franken then asked if he could speak to the superior of the Pakistani. This turned out to be another Pakistani, and he also repeatedly insisted that the OPs in question were not on his map in Tuzla. In short, the BSA could not attack OPs which did not exist. As a result, the request for air support was flat-out rejected by the two Pakistanis." Thank you. Have I read that out correctly and is what it says here correct? And what can you say to explain all this to us, because it doesn't seem to be very clear.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to me it's quite clear. You read it correctly. It's exactly what it said. The first officer I got on the radio was the acting chief OPS room of the Sector North-east, and because I, let's say, almost lost my temper, I asked for his superior, which was the G-3 head of the section, G-3 head of the section operations of the Sector North-east in Tuzla. But he also stated that I didn't have these OPs, et cetera, et cetera. So what is mentioned there, what is written down there is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that perhaps a convenient time for the second break? We are over time already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we will have our second break now, and resume at 1.00. Perhaps before we rise, could you indicate if you could conclude your cross-examination today of is it not possible?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I believe that we shall have to continue tomorrow, because I still have some questions to ask. That is to say, we'll continue on the next working day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is next week. We resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Based on what we saw a while ago in e-court, I would like to ask you this: Did you, as the deputy battalion commander of UNPROFOR in Srebrenica, have the right to request air support?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a deputy commander, I would have had when the commander was not present, but as being the acting S3, which means operations officer, of the battalion, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the battalion the level that decided on air support or did they -- that have to be decided by some other command level in UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The battalion was a level that asked for it because they needed it and the decision whether it was given or not is a higher level within UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How much time elapsed between your request and the decision to launch air-strikes against the forces that you had requested?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the UN situation, at least hours, because this decision had to be made on very high level. I understood that even the Secretary-General had to give his opinion or his consent. So that took at least hours before there was a consent for air support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I apologise. I didn't see you earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's quite all right, Mr. President. I was just going to suggest if these types of questions proceed further along this line, then perhaps a reference to a particular occasion might be more helpful. I understand the last question may have been general and generated a general answer, but as we've heard, there were several requests for close air support during the course of these events. So if we're going to go further, I would just suggest that maybe the Colonel's attention be pointed towards a specific request.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In compliance with the request by the Prosecution can you tell us when was the first time when you requested close air support and on which targets was it directed specifically?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First time we requested air support was during the attack of the VRS on OP Echo, the observation post in the south that fell on the 3rd of June. Target was the main battle tank and the infantry then more or less gathered in the -- in the wood factory and the surroundings of OP Echo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ask for support on the 3rd, and did that occur on that same day or did that happen later?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I asked for the support on the 3rd, the very moment that attack showed or occurred. That's an answer to your question, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there an immediate air support against those mortars? Again, I'm asking you how long was it between your request and the air-strikes that ensued?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring again to the situation on OP Echo, there was no air support. It was denied. And in general, I could say the only time that it was we got air support was much later, on the 11th of July, in the area of the city of Srebrenica. Every request we did before was denied with various reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us now move to the one that wasn't denied. At what time did you file this request on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I must stretch my answer a bit. On the 10th we got the message that we would be supported by massive air support on the 11th. I then had my ops officer make a request for an air-strike on the 11th. Air-strike is what I pointed out before. Not one target but trying to -- to fight all known targets in one time. The first message was that we would get that air-strike supported by 44 aeroplanes. Then the very moment that it would be effective, 0600 hours in the morning of the 11th, they didn't come. The close air support that was, as far as I recollect, on the 11th, about 1300 hours, that came in, was the remains of that manned air-strike. So I didn't specifically ask for that close air support mission, but we found out, and that's the procedure, our forward air controller got contact with two F16s and led him -- led them to the target on the ground. Is that an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us now, what was the reason for not using on a great scale the aircraft starting at 0600 hours?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have the faintest idea. It was announced to us. We took measures to support that, to facilitate that, and then they didn't come. The message we got, mission aborted. That's a technical -- military technical word, but that meant the order to all the planes to return home. And how later on those two Dutch F16 fighters did come in and did one CAS mission, close air support mission, I didn't know, but we were happy with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please -- can you please tell us, was that pursuant to your request that the operation would start at 0600 hours, or was it something that they decided? And I'm talking about this time line.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my request was ASAP, that means as soon as possible, because our modern means can perform actions like that by night as well. And they, meaning higher command UN, made the deadline 600 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ask for specific targets to be stricken or did you just ask for a blanket support?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the risk that it is getting technical, but we did both, in fact. We gave all the hardware -- sorry, all the known targets being guns and artillery and mortars and tanks, et cetera, we put them on the list and gave them a free-for-all, a killing zone, so to say, directly south of Srebrenica, and that is the area between the city of Srebrenica and generally Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This means that it did not pertain to the then current situation, but you wanted massive strikes against the targets that you perceived as being dangerous for you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was not in contradiction with the current situation. My aim with the targets I gave with the air-strikes is to take out all known VRS artillery and tanks positions, and being the approach from the south, the main approach, the main effort of the VRS in our direction, that's why I gave that area to the planes, just to fight and destroy anything they found there. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, when did you issue the green order?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That must have been the evening of the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that, from then on, your soldiers had no restrictions with respect to the use of the weapons that they had at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you inform the Muslims that you had issued such an order on the 9th and that your army was to be engaged alongside them in the defence of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did inform the Muslims that we would take or would start actually to defend Srebrenica. And the second remark, that our army was engaged alongside them in the defence of Srebrenica, was not said to them. The CO of DutchBat had a meeting with the staff of the 28th Division that night and he informed them, not only about our defending the city but as well about the air-strike who, in our opinion, was evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Starting from the evening of the 9th onwards, you acted alongside them against the same targets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We acted occasionally alongside them, but we acted against the same targets, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that period until the 11th, when the first air-strikes occurred, did you suffer any losses in the activities launched by the VRS in self-defence? And I'm talking about the period between the 9th and the 11th.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you be more specific with regard to the losses?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, we had several injured, lightly injured. We had, as I recollect well, three APCs not operationable anymore by fire, and as I recollect well, about two light vehicles destroyed. Or destroyed is the wrong way. Damaged in a way that they were not usable anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from those lightly injured and the damaged vehicles, were any losses incurred by you by the VRS between the 9th and the 11th, when the first air-strikes were launched and when you issued the green order?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand the question correctly is whether I have knowledge of losses at the side of the VRS in that period. I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: No. I didn't ask you about the losses incurred by the VRS. I'm asking about your losses in the period between the 9th when you issued the green order and NATO strikes against the Army of Republika Srpska. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I stated before, I had some injured men, but I had no deadly losses, if that is the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank God that that is what happened, because you were engaged fighting the VRS for the whole of two days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That's correct. We were lucky.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether the UNPROFOR forces became a legitimate target starting from the 9th? Were they entitled, did they have the right to shoot at you? Did you realise that you would become a legitimate target once you opened fire on them together with the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, you said "were they entitled, did they have the right to shoot at you?" I'm a very happy guy. UNPROFOR didn't shoot at me, but you mean probably the right to shoot at the VRS. Well, I stated that before. Yes, we were in a state of war towards the VRS, and we opened fire together with the Muslim army. You're saying that again and again. The Muslims were fighting the VRS as well, but this supposes some kind of co-ordination on any level, and again there was no such co-ordination otherwise as the initial appointment we made -- agreement we made in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you realise at that point that the VRS had issued an order not to shoot at UNPROFOR? Did you know that that was the case before you issued your order, and that is to say that they had issued their order on the 8th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did -- I do not realise that, and I must say that not everybody followed that order. That's clear. And I mean, not everyone followed the -- not all the of the VRS followed that order, if it was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's possible, but did you know that General Gobillard talked to the Main Staff, and was information provided by the Main Staff to Gobillard to you, passed on to you, and that the Main Staff asked our forces to describe those locations and that they were told to target them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the question? It was not clear to the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you were asked by the interpreters to repeat your question because it was not clear to them, for proper translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you, as members in -- of UNPROFOR in Srebrenica, informed by your Sarajevo command that the Main Staff was claiming that their soldiers were being shot at from UNPROFOR vehicles and from observation posts of UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. I was not informed that way. But they didn't have to inform me, because I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what was it that you knew.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a situation like that, your command radio only gives you a tactical information. So if the company, B Company, for instance, gave the message, "We have contact at position whatever," that meant that there was fire contact not only with the VRS but in probably in any or many or all cases, which I didn't know of because I wasn't present on every spot, fire was responded by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we heard from you earlier, as you said yourself, you were at war with the VRS starting from the 9th of July until the withdrawal to Potocari, and you said that the only losses you incurred was a number of lightly injures -- injured soldiers and that two armoured vehicles and three light vehicles were damaged. So after that period, were you informed by your Sarajevo command and General Gobillard, who maintained communication with the Main Staff of the VRS, about the guarantees given by the VRS that they would not be targeting you any longer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you see an order that we looked at a moment ago which Ivanovic directly forwarded to all the units, which I wrote, to tell them not to shoot at UNPROFOR members? So did you see that the Army of Republika Srpska issued such orders? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's one of the documents I saw before, but then again obviously not everybody obeyed those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did we have -- did you have reports from your observation posts that they were being -- that they weren't targeting them despite your green order on the 9th, 10th and 11th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that my observation posts or positions reported that while being under fire of the VRS they didn't reply -- respond that fire? Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You issued an order, and you said that it was a state of war. However, what I'm asking you is whether there were any cases, specific cases, whereby you received reports from the OPs that the Army of Republika Srpska wasn't killing them, wasn't shooting at them, but was passing by and leaving them behind their own positions because they didn't want to kill them or inflict losses. That's what I'm asking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I understand the question now. Yeah, there were several reports that OPs, without knowing that the ABiH left their positions, were amidst the VRS forces, and then the situation came that they surrendered to the VRS. And there was in those cases not an attempt to kill them or shoot at them, because they were outmanoeuvred and, in fact, militarily seen, useless, and they became POW.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us now whether the VRS took them -- captured them when they surrendered or were they allowed to go to the base at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not allowed to go to Potocari. They were taken, escorted by the VRS to the area of Bratunac in most cases. Couple of other crews were held in the mining area, and then through -- as far as I know, through Milici to Bratunac. But they were not free to go. The only event where that happened was at OP Foxtrot, when they were surrounded and they tried -- they waited for a pause in the firing to withdraw. They were too late and they were surrounded by VRS, and then they said, We want to go back. And they had to leave their light weapons and could return, and that's when, in their return, the killing of soldier van Renssen took place. But the rest all was escorted to Bratunac or another location.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, could you just tell us -- well, you said the killing of soldiers. Who killed them, the BH Army or the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referred to the -- the killing of soldier van Renssen, being a member of the crew of OP Foxtrot who was shot by the ABiH in -- during the retreat to the camp in Srebrenica. We spoke about that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the Army of Republika Srpska, did it demand that any UNPROFOR members who were there from the 9th, when you issued the green order, to the end in the conflict with the army, did they ask that they be prisoners of war or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, the question is that -- whether the VRS asked to whom, whether those crews of the OPs in Bratunac were POWs; is that correct? Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was this: Did the Army of Republika Srpska demand of UNPROFOR that these soldiers in Bratunac that were excluded from the fighting should be held accountable as prisoners of war for the losses they inflicted in their actions on the 9th, 10th and 11th to the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't account or -- sorry. You can't hold a POW accountable for the losses he inflicted on you. So I don't understand what that question should be. And they were declared POW literally by the VRS in one of their ultimatums after the air attack on the 11th. They themselves declared them POW. And "they themselves," I mean the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it logical for you to exclude somebody from combat so that they could not incur losses and to proclaim them prisoners of war? Was that legitimate? Or should they have freed them and allowed them to go back to their positions and back into combat and do some more shooting? That's my question and I'd like your answer.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Of course a POW, you keep them and you don't send them back to your opponent. So it's legitimate to declare them POW and keep them in custody according to the rules like Geneva Convention, et cetera. There's no question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just tell me this, please: When those air-strikes occurred on the 11th, and when the Dutch planes went into action, those that set out at 6.00, were they in the air?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have contact with them, but I understood that somewhere in the morning afterwards, when I was back in Holland and had my own debrief with the air force, I understood that during the morning the rest of the planes were aborted mission. That meant they had to return to their original airfields. So the other planes were, as far as I know, not in the air. And again, it was not -- that action was not an air-strike, but just for the record, that is a close air support mission of those two fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So those are the two Dutch planes. But when there were mass strikes, they said -- you said they gave up and returned. When they returned, it means they went back to base, to the destinations they were located in to begin with. Do you know anything about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know exactly where they went, but that is the normal procedure. Just to be sure to be clear for the Court as well, if you plan an air-strikes, you plan a holding area. All the planes committed in that air-strike gather there. They're flying around, in fact. And then on command or on the time ordered, they leave that holding area and perform or execute that action. During the stay in the holding area of those 44 planes, I understood the order was given to those planes abort mission. That means that they flew out of the holding area and went back to their respective airfields where they came from. If the next question is why those two F16s stayed and performed that close air support mission, I really don't know. I was happy with it, but I don't know why they stayed, whether that was on order. It must have been. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now tell us, because we're drawing to a close, the end of the working day and this session, that had there been mass support by planes, as you put it, would you then consider that UNPROFOR, honing positions in Srebrenica, Zepa and other places, had taken sides, and would that have violated the mandate you were given? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to make that clear before. The fact that I was ordered to defend the city of Srebrenica and that area, in fact, has nothing to do with taking a side. If I had that order to defend it to the ABiH, I would have done that as well. The eventuality that the ABiH in this case had the same enemy is as it is. So if those air-strikes were performed as planned and as asked for by me, the only result would have been that I think that I would have been able to defend the city of Srebrenica at least longer as I could now. Is that an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during your mandate, did you have the task of defending one of the parties in the conflict? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My original orders were to deter any party for military action by presence and so on, facilitate the work of -- facilitate humanitarian air -- aid, et cetera, improve the condition within the enclave. So that was my original order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During the trial so far, we were told that it -- that the Muslim army was given to understand in Srebrenica that there would be a mass aeroplane operation and that they should clear out a certain area. Can you tell us more about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact words I do not know, because that was given to them, told to them by my CO, Colonel Karremans, at night, somewhere in the city of Srebrenica itself, and he did. That is what I know --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Give us the date, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That must have been the late evening of the 10th that he was there and that he informed them about the air-strike situation. And I presume, but it is a presumption, that he informed them that they better had to be away from the killing zone, and pointed out to them, otherwise, they would have a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether that was co-ordination and co-operation between your command and commanders with the forces of one of the parties to the conflict? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it more as information about things to happen. We did not -- or did he not suggest or make mutual plans, so plans for both parties, to cope with the problem we were both facing, being the VRS. Then it, in my view, would be co-ordination, co-operation. He just informed them what UNPROFOR was -- sorry, what our battalion was doing -- was going to do, and informed them about the air support and consequences for the killing zone, and it wouldn't be wise to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As they were told that, after you issued the green order and when you became involved in the war conflict with one of the sides, can that then be considered to be co-ordination and harmonisation of action in the air and on the ground? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's more or less the same case that you put in your former question. No. We informed them that we are going to defend the city of Srebrenica, and as far is there any co-ordination or whatever, it's only the consequence of the agreement we made in March. At that very moment, there hasn't been any military co-ordination, because that would mean, for instance, that on the ground -- I'm getting technical now, but on the ground we would say, okay, this house is the left border of our defence. You take the next house. That is your sector where -- in which you fire. This is my sector, et cetera. You got antitank weapons. Okay. Concentrate them on that road. That is co-ordination. The simple fact that we informed them that we are going or we were ordered to defend the city of Srebrenica has nothing to do with co-operation or co-ordination in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And before we conclude, I have one more question. One of your mandates was to disarm the BH Army. Just give me a short answer, please. The BH Army in Srebrenica that is. Yes or no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of my missions, and we failed to do that, to be complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And was it within your mandate to destroy the weapons of the Army of Republika Srpska and to go to war with the VRS after the green order had been issued? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not within the mandate, but then again, my mandate was changed significantly the very moment the UN ordered me to defend Srebrenica, and that was the cause why I gave that green order in that sequence it was. So there's a period of mandate being till the order of the UN to my battalion to defend the city, and after that, the rules of engagement, et cetera, all restrictions on the use of weapons, were gone because that goes with the order to defend something. I can't defend something by sweetly talking with everybody and standing -- just standing there. I had to use and was authorised to use my weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether that mandate was changed by the United Nations in the Security Council giving you the right to go into action against one of the parties to the conflict? Thank you. And was that verified by any Resolution that followed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know, and to say bluntly, I don't care. I got my orders. I am a soldier. I'm on the ground. I got orders from my next higher echelon. Obviously legitimate orders, and then I follow my orders. And whether the Security Council or whoever wants to speak about it, discuss it or whatever, I did not care in that very moment. Simply, soldier follow orders. As long as the orders doesn't, for me, obvious, make me -- in any way make me doing criminal acts, I followed those orders and I perform them as best I can. It is as difficult and as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. As a number of acts were committed, some people were killed, some suffered in another way and so on and so forth, does that imply that this must have been backed up by somebody having given a verification, corroboration? I understand you. You went into action, as you said, because you were in a conflict of war with the VRS, and it's commendable that as an officer you carried out our orders. But I would like to know who it is who was responsible for issuing the order and for the fact that UNPROFOR was placed or took sides, that UNPROFOR took sides and went into action together with one side against another side? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I do not agree with you concerning your conclusion that UNPROFOR took side, as far as my battalion is concerned. I explained that again and again that I don't think what we did was taking a side. And I do not know what level or who did initiate the order to DutchBat to defend the city. The only thing I know is that my next higher echelon ordered me to do so, et cetera, et cetera. I explained how I think about that before to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In order to prevent a repetition of these questions again, at least today, we are running out of time and we have to adjourn, Mr. Tolimir and everybody else. We will adjourn and resume next week on Tuesday, in the afternoon, in this courtroom, 2.15. I would like to remind you again not to contact the parties on the content of your testimony. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 6th day of July, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.51 p.m.,
